Network Intrusion Detection Adaptability under Spurious Labels: A Noise-Aware Few-Shot
Class-Incremental Learning FrameworkThanks:  Z. Zhao and Y. Abstract

Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDSs) must incrementally adapt to emerging attacks, even when only a limited amount of labeled network traffic is available. Consequently, Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning (FSCIL)-based NIDSs have gained growing attention. However, existing FSCIL-based NIDSs are highly vulnerable to label noise in newly-observed attack classes. To address this limitation, we propose NAFN, a noise-aware FSCIL-based NIDS framework that reduces the impact of mislabeled data during incremental adaptation. NAFN consists of two components: (i) Noise Detection, which identifies and removes mislabeled biflows using noise-detection algorithms, and (ii) Feature Sampling, which estimates class-conditional embeddings from clean biflows, calibrates them with base-class statistics, and resamples synthetic features to recover the original biflow count. The framework follows the Rethink Few-Shot (RFS) teacher–student paradigm with lightweight nearest-neighbor or logistic regression classifiers, and various pretraining & memory selection strategies. Experiments on CSE-CIC-IDS2018, Edge-IIoT, and IoT-NID datasets show that NAFN effectively preserves prior knowledge and maintains strong incremental performance even under 50% label noise, consistently improving new-class F1-scores over non-denoised baselines, up to +𝟓𝟐%\bm{+52\%}, while being time-efficient and robust in cross-network and high-noise incremental settings. The implementation is publicly available to foster reproducibility.

Index Terms: 
Network Intrusion Detection System, Few-Shot Learning, Class-Incremental Learning, Network Security, Label Noise.

I Introduction

Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDSs) play a critical role in safeguarding network security by monitoring traffic and detecting malicious activities. As intrusion techniques become increasingly sophisticated, NIDSs have evolved from early approaches based on port analysis and deep packet inspection to modern detection methods based on Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) [30]. However, traditional ML & DL-based NIDSs are typically trained on closed-world datasets, containing only known benign and attack traffic. In real-world network environments, however, new attacks continually emerge. Recent threat-intelligence reports confirm this trend, driven by ransomware and AI-enabled malicious campaigns. For instance, in Oct. 20252025, organizations worldwide faced an average of 1,9381,938 cyberattacks per week, an increase of 2%2\% over the previous month and 5%5\% compared to Oct. 20242024 [32]. Consequently, NIDSs struggle to adapt to this ever-changing threat landscape, resulting in limited effectiveness in real deployments. To address this limitation, recent works have explored Class-Incremental Learning (𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{CIL})-based NIDSs [37, 52] to continually learn new attacks while retaining previously acquired knowledge. Nonetheless, 𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{CIL} suffers from the scarcity of labeled traffic samples for new attacks, particularly in the case of zero-day attacks. The integration of Few-Shot Learning (𝙵𝚂𝙻\mathtt{FSL}) [54, 53] with 𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{CIL}—i.e. Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning (𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL})—has emerged as a promising research direction for attack-traffic detection. 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL}-based NIDSs aim to incrementally classify new attacks with only a few labeled traffic samples (viz. few shots) without losing performance on previously learned classes.

Despite promising progress [9, 11, 7], existing 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL}-based NIDS remain fragile in real-world network environments. Most studies assume that the few available samples from new attacks are accurately labeled, which rarely holds true. Unlike base-class datasets that are carefully collected and labeled in controlled settings, new-class attack samples are often gathered from uncontrolled network environments where labels are generated through heuristic rules, automated scripts, or weak supervision, making them prone to errors. Hence, label noise can severely degrade the performance of 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL}-based NIDS. Since each new attack class contains only a few labeled traffic samples, every mislabeled instance can severely distort the feature distribution, degrading detection performance and introducing classification bias [50]. In contrast, large-sample learning can tolerate noise as its influence is diluted [33]. Although manual relabeling can mitigate this problem, it is costly and undermines the real-time responsiveness required for intrusion detection. Therefore, label noise remains a major challenge that limits the robustness and practical deployment of 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL}-based NIDS.

In this paper, we propose 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN}, a Noise-Aware FSCIL-based NIDS framework designed to mitigate label noise and enhance robustness in real-world scenarios. 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} introduces a Noise-Aware Module, consisting of two components: (i) noise detection and (ii) feature sampling. Specifically, the noise detector removes mislabeled traffic samples from new attacks, while the feature sampler generates calibrated embeddings from the remaining clean data to mitigate the impact of sample loss. Since this component is designed as a modular part of 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN}, it can accommodate different noise detection methods. To determine the most suitable choice, we evaluate several candidates, including Local Outlier Factor, Isolation Forest, Example-Level Curriculum Learning, and Prototype-Margin strategy. Ultimately, we adopt Prototype-Margin as the default option due to its superior stability and accuracy. For feature sampling, the module estimates the feature distribution of clean new-class samples (after noise detection) and generates new embeddings based on this distribution. To alleviate distribution bias under few-shot conditions, inspired by the literature on 𝙵𝚂𝙻\mathtt{FSL} [46], we further introduce a distribution calibration mechanism that leverages statistics from the base classes to align feature distributions of new and existing classes, thereby improving stability and generalization.

𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} is trained in two stages. First, a base training phase, and then multiple incremental learning phases. During the base training phase, the model learns from the initial classes. When new attacks appear, 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} performs incremental learning to quickly adapt. We adopt the Rethinking Few-Shot (𝚁𝙵𝚂\mathtt{RFS}) approach [39], tailored to incremental learning [9], as the core mechanism enabling 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} to adapt to new attacks. 𝚁𝙵𝚂\mathtt{RFS} employs a teacher–student distillation strategy: at each incremental phase, the model from the previous phase acts as the teacher to guide the student, while a small set of samples from old classes (viz. memory) is retained to prevent forgetting. This design enables rapid adaptation to new attacks while maintaining knowledge stability. To further enhance the representation capability of the base model, we explore several pretraining strategies, including reconstruction-based [54, 23], contrastive [16, 25], and hybrid methods [44]. In addition, we propose 𝙼𝚎𝚖​+\mathtt{Mem}\text{+}, which integrates various exemplar selection strategies to populate the memory. We consider the following strategies: Herding [31], Rainbow [3], and Random Sampling. To summarize, our main contributions are as follows.

  • •

    We propose 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN}, a Noise-Aware Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning framework for Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS). It enables continual adaptation to novel attacks with few samples while effectively mitigating catastrophic forgetting, thus fulfilling the core goal of 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL}-based NIDS. Experiments on three benchmark datasets (𝙲𝚂𝙴​-​𝙲𝙸𝙲​-​𝙸𝙳𝚂𝟸𝟶𝟷𝟾\mathtt{CSE\text{-}CIC\text{-}IDS2018}, 𝙴𝚍𝚐𝚎​-​𝙸𝙸𝚘𝚃\mathtt{Edge\text{-}IIoT}, and 𝙸𝚘𝚃​-​𝙽𝙸𝙳\mathtt{IoT\text{-}NID}) demonstrate that 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} achieves superior performance in incremental adaptation.

  • •

    We design a pluggable Noise-Aware Module to mitigate the impact of label noise. This module can identify and remove label noise in new attack traffic and generate new feature embeddings to restore the original data size. Under label noise conditions (noise levels ranging from 10%10\% to 50%50\%), experimental results show a significant performance improvement in F1-score for new attacks, up to +52%+52\% w.r.t. the baseline without denoising strategies.

  • •

    We perform a comprehensive evaluation of 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} under both individual and combined challenges of cross-network adaptation and label noise. The results show that 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} achieves consistent and generalizable performance across heterogeneous network datasets and remains robust under severe noise, with the largest observed pAUC improvements reaching 13%13\% for new attacks and 11%11\% for previously unseen attacks in high-noise settings.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Sec. II reviews recent works relevant to our study and positions our contribution within the existing literature. Sec. III formalizes the problem of label noise on 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL}-based NIDSs and defines our research questions and objectives. Sec. IV provides an overview of 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} and details each of its components. Sec. V describes the experimental setup, while Sec. VI presents a comprehensive evaluation of 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} on three recent and public datasets. Finally, Sec. VII ends the paper.

II Related Works

Background. In recent years, there has been growing research interest in applying ML, and later DL, as the core of AI-based NIDS [15]. Following this first wave, the research community has shifted its focus to addressing the main limitations of ML & DL [37, 10, 24]. Two challenges are particularly relevant, (i) poor performance against network attacks that were not seen during training [37, 52]; (ii) difficulty of gathering and labeling high-quality and up-to-date datasets, which leads to class imbalance, and, consequently, unsatisfactory results [54, 53]. To mitigate the first issue (i), 𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{CIL} has emerged as a promising direction. Unlike conventional training, where models are retrained from scratch when new classes appear, 𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{CIL} seeks to incrementally integrate new knowledge without forgetting. 𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{CIL} approaches typically rely on strategies such as rehearsal, regularization, or dynamic architectures [26]. 𝙵𝚂𝙻\mathtt{FSL} has shown potential in dealing with the second issue (ii). 𝙵𝚂𝙻\mathtt{FSL} focuses on enabling models to generalize from a limited number of labeled samples by leveraging prior knowledge acquired from related tasks. 𝙵𝚂𝙻\mathtt{FSL} approaches typically rely on metric-learning, prototype-based classification, or meta-learning [43]. Efforts to integrate 𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{CIL} and 𝙵𝚂𝙻\mathtt{FSL}—i.e. 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL}—remain relatively underexplored in current literature [9, 11, 7], despite its practical advantages (e.g., rapid adaptation to new threats). In the computer vision domain, 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL} has been more extensively investigated [38, 55, 41]. The common goal is to prepare models to recognize new classes by exploiting knowledge from previously learned ones. Existing approaches mainly differ in how they allocate and adapt the representation space. For instance, Tao et al. [38] propose a growing Neural Gas Network that dynamically expands its structure to accommodate new classes. Similarly, Zhou et al. [55] reserve embedding space in advance by assigning multiple virtual prototypes. More recently, Wang et al. [41] observe that new-class samples are often misclassified into semantically similar old classes. They leverage this property by calibrating new class prototypes through weighted combinations of old prototypes. In the field of network intrusion detection, 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL} still faces critical challenges. Particularly, their reliance on only a few labeled samples for adapting to new traffic classes makes them highly vulnerable to label noise. Such noise may arise unintentionally (e.g., labeling in non-controlled environments) or through adversarial manipulation (e.g., label-flipping attacks). Although the literature on label noise in non-𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL} contexts is growing [1, 48], the availability of larger datasets in these contexts partially mitigates its impact, making it less critical than in 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL} scenarios.

Literature Review. Table I categorizes the most relevant works that employ 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL} and address the label noise problem. Research on 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL} is still in its early stages; the first contribution was proposed in 20212021 [42], while most subsequent works appeared between 20242024 and 20252025 [45, 17, 5, 7, 9]. Studies that address label noise in the context of NIDS remain relatively limited, reflecting the novelty of this research effort [1, 48, 47, 14, 27, 49]. Notably, to the best of our knowledge, no existing work has yet tackled label noise within the 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL} setting.

Among the FSCIL approaches explored in the literature, the most common is Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) [13], originally designed for 𝙵𝚂𝙻\mathtt{FSL} applications. Works adopting MAML [42, 45, 5] extend it with strategies to handle forgetting and add new classes. In particular, Wang et al. [42] enable MAML for 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL} through a model growth technique. Wang et al. [45] use Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) to alleviate forgetting by selecting models with similar feature distributions. Cao et al. [5] adopt memory replay of previous classes during the incremental task. Unlike the aforementioned works, Du et al. [11] adapt Prototypical Networks (PN) [36] to 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL} using memory replay [5] and introduce session-specific projection layers to improve traffic-feature discriminability. Cerasuolo et al. [7] evaluate several 𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{CIL} approaches from computer vision and traffic classification under few-shot constraints. In our previous work [9], we adapt a set of 𝙵𝚂𝙻\mathtt{FSL} approaches to 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL} by integrating memory replay to mitigate forgetting.

Regarding denoising approaches, state-of-the-art works can be grouped into two strategies. The first aims to build models robust to spurious labels. Yuan et al. [48] design both the model architecture and the loss function to enhance robustness. They employ an Autoencoder coupled with a K-Means to cluster samples in unsupervised fashion, thus reducing the impact of noisy annotations. A Boundary Augmentation Loss is then introduced to regularize decision boundaries. Similarly, Zhan et al. [49] use K-Means to detect noisy labels and correct them based on prediction confidence. They use a Transformer encoder-only for noise robustness. Hallaji et al. [14] adopt a generative approach to inject artificial noise, training classifiers on perturbed samples, viz. vaccination.

The second strategy of works focuses on correcting mislabeled samples. Specifically, Abrishami et al. [1] use Decision Trees to detect potential label errors, assuming minority labels in a leaf are likely incorrect, and leverage Active Learning to have humans verify uncertain cases. Yuan et al. [47] and Meng et al. [27] both leverage local density and feature similarity to identify reliable prototypes for relabeling. In both papers, samples are reassigned based on their similarity to class prototypes. Yuan et al. [47] introduce a custom loss to preserve class separability, while Meng et al. [27] refine prototype selection by choosing high-density yet diverse samples.

Table I highlights that the current literature lacks systematic cross-network analyses [2, 10] in 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL} and label noise scenarios (e.g., models are trained on one dataset, representing a network environment, and tested on another, or incremental classes belong to a different dataset than the one used for pretraining). The only exception [9] performs a cross-network incremental analysis for 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL} approaches. To the best of our knowledge, no existing work addresses cross-network studies under noisy-label conditions.

Regarding the datasets, we observe that 𝙲𝙸𝙲​-​𝙸𝙳𝚂𝟸𝟶𝟷𝟽\mathtt{CIC}\text{-}\mathtt{IDS2017} and 𝙲𝚂𝙴​-​𝙲𝙸𝙲​-​𝙸𝙳𝚂𝟸𝟶𝟷𝟾\mathtt{CSE\text{-}CIC\text{-}IDS2018} are among the most popular choices [11, 48, 47, 45, 5, 27, 9]. Several IoT-oriented datasets are also frequently adopted (i.e. 𝙸𝚘𝚃​-​𝟸𝟹\mathtt{IoT\text{-}23}, 𝙸𝚘𝚃​-​𝙽𝙸𝙳\mathtt{IoT\text{-}NID}, and 𝙴𝚍𝚐𝚎​-​𝙸𝙸𝚘𝚃\mathtt{Edge\text{-}IIoT} [1, 48, 7, 9]). While 𝙽𝚂𝙻​-​𝙺𝙳𝙳\mathtt{NSL\text{-}KDD} remains popular [42, 47, 17], despite being over two decades old, it no longer reflects modern network traffic and offers limited relevance for evaluating contemporary NIDS.

Table I also flags the studies that employ raw input [11, 48, 7, 9, 49], i.e. unprocessed network data, in contrast to handcrafted or statistical features. Raw input is naturally aligned with DL approaches, which are capable of automatically extracting meaningful representations. On the other hand, works that rely on statistical features introduce additional pre-processing steps, increasing computational overhead. Furthermore, they weaken the “promise” of end-to-end DL pipelines requiring little or no human intervention.

Finally, the table marks the works adopting an early input strategy [11, 7, 9, 49]. This approach leverages only the initial portion of a traffic object (e.g., the first packets or bytes of the payload) as input, enabling early detection. Remaining works, instead, rely on the entire traffic object, making them suitable only for post-mortem detection, which is effective for offline analysis but unsuitable for live network scenarios.

Positioning. The last row of Table I positions our work against the reviewed literature. Building on our previous work [9], which compared multiple 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL} approaches, we explore different training and adaptation optimizations for 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL}-based NIDS, including improved pre-training stages and memory selection criteria (referred to as 𝙼𝚎𝚖​+\mathtt{Mem}\text{+}). Unlike the literature leveraging MAML for 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL}, which is known for its high computational cost and slow adaptation [29], our method builds upon the more efficient 𝚁𝙵𝚂\mathtt{RFS} [39]. In our prior study [9], 𝚁𝙵𝚂\mathtt{RFS} delivered the best performance and is better suited for real-world NIDS deployments. Furthermore, it differs from Wang et al. [45], which adopts a model selection strategy requiring the storage of multiple candidate models, thereby limiting scalability. 𝚁𝙵𝚂\mathtt{RFS} also differs from 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL} based on PN [11], whose performance strongly depends on the quality of the learned prototypes. Existing works reveals two main gaps concerning label noise: (i) the lack of studies addressing label noise within the 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL} setting, and (ii) the absence of comparative analyses across denoising strategies. We address both gaps by systematically evaluating and comparing multiple denoising approaches under 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL} . Moreover, we ground our denoising strategy, based on filtering and synthesizing clean biflows, in the findings of [19]. In real-world NIDS deployments, the true noise ratio is unknown, making over-cleaning a realistic risk. Under these conditions, Jiang et al. [19] show that filtering significantly outperforms correction. The main limitation of filtering is the reduced sample size, which can increase the generalization error bound; our feature sampling module mitigates this effect. This distinguishes our approach from prior works based on label correction [27, 47, 1]. Equally important, we conduct a cross-network incremental study on both 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL} and label noise scenarios across three recent and publicly-available datasets. All experiments are performed on raw and early input data to ensure realistic and low-latency NIDS.

III Problem Formalization & Research Objectives

In this section, we formalize 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL} and label noise in the context of NIDS. Next, we present the research objectives of our proposed framework, 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN}.

FSCIL Formalization. The goal of a 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL}-based NIDS is to continuously adapt to new attack classes using only a few labeled samples, while preserving high classification performance on previously learned classes. Formally, the base training phase refers to training the model on the class set 𝒞base\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{base}}, which includes benign traffic and a set of known attack classes. Each base class contains an average of N¯base\bar{N}_{\mathrm{base}} labeled samples for training, where N¯base\bar{N}_{\mathrm{base}} denotes the average number of samples per base class. This phase produces the initial (base) model used for subsequent incremental learning phases. During each incremental phase t∈{1,2,…}t\in\{1,2,\ldots\}, a new set of attack classes 𝒞new(t)\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{new}} appears, corresponding to previously unseen attacks:

𝒞new(t)∩𝒞old(t)=∅,where ​𝒞old(t)=𝒞base∪⋃i=1t−1𝒞new(i).\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{new}}\cap\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{old}}=\emptyset,\quad\text{where }\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{old}}=\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{base}}\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{t-1}\mathcal{C}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{new}}. (1)

This condition ensures that each incremental phase involves previously unseen attack classes. Each new class c∈𝒞new(t)c\in\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{new}} contains only a small number of KK labeled samples, where K≪N¯baseK\ll\bar{N}_{\mathrm{base}}. The primary challenge of 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL} in the context of NIDS is to achieve rapid adaptation to newly emerging attacks in 𝒞new(t)\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{new}} while preserving high classification performance on previously learned classes in 𝒞old(t)\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{old}}.

Label Noise Formalization. In a real-world 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL}-based NIDS setting, the limited samples available for new attacks 𝒞new(t)\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{new}} are often affected by label noise. Let the attack dataset for incremental phase tt be

𝒟new(t)={(𝒙i,y~i)}i=1N(t),\mathcal{D}_{\text{new}}^{(t)}=\{(\bm{x}_{i},\tilde{y}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N^{(t)}}, (2)

with y~i∈𝒞new(t)\tilde{y}_{i}\in\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{new}} the observed (possibly noisy) label of attack sample 𝒙i\bm{x}_{i}. For clarity, let yiy_{i} denote the ground-truth label. Since each new class c∈𝒞new(t)c\in\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{new}} contains only KK labeled samples, the total number of samples for the phase is N(t)=K×|𝒞new(t)|N^{(t)}=K\times|\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{new}}|. Label noise occurs when y~i≠yi\tilde{y}_{i}\neq y_{i}, e.g., when a sample from attack class c1c_{1} is mislabeled as attack c2c_{2}. The noise rate η\eta is defined as

η=1N(t)∑i=1N(t)𝕀[y~i≠yi],\eta=\frac{1}{N^{(t)}}\sum_{i=1}^{N^{(t)}}\mathbb{I}[\tilde{y}_{i}\neq y_{i}], (3)

where 𝕀⁡[⋅]\mathbb{I[\cdot]} is the indicator function. Note that label noise is symmetrically distributed across classes in 𝒞new(t)\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{new}}. Given the small number of samples for each new attack class, even a small noise rate η\eta can significantly degrade the discriminative power of the model. Thus, the central challenge addressed in this paper lies in achieving stable incremental learning under the dual constraints of few-shot data and label noise.

Research Questions & Objectives. Building upon the identified challenges, this work formulates the following research questions and their corresponding objectives, centered around the proposed Noise-Aware 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL}-based NIDS (𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN}).

 Can 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} address the primary challenge of 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL} by effectively adapting to new attack classes while retaining previously acquired knowledge?

 How robust is 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} to label noise, and how effective are its integrated noise detection and feature calibration mechanisms in mitigating the impact of mislabeled samples?

 Can 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} maintain stable and generalizable performance when adapting across different networks, and remain robust when facing the combined challenges of cross-network adaptation and label noise?

IV Methodology

In this section, we present the overall methodology of 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN}, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Particularly, we describe 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} from three complementary perspectives:

  1. i)

    NIDS Workflow (Horizontal Process). The end-to-end data pipeline—composed of Flow Processor, Feature Encoder, and Attack-Traffic Classifier—transforms raw network traffic into feature embeddings and labels traffic in benign and attack classes (Sec. IV-A).

  2. ii)

    Learning Procedure (Vertical Process). Describes how 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} learns across tasks via Base Training and Incremental Learning phases, following the teacher–student paradigm. The Memory Update mechanism (𝙼𝚎𝚖​+\mathtt{Mem}\text{+}) preserves representative samples to reduce catastrophic forgetting (Sec. IV-B).

  3. iii)

    Noise-Aware Module. In addition to these two main processes, 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} includes the Noise-Aware Module that operates exclusively during the incremental learning phase. It detects mislabeled samples of new attacks and synthesizes calibrated embeddings to maintain clean training data (Sec. IV-C).

By integrating these perspectives—the horizontal workflow, the vertical learning procedure, and the Noise-Aware Module—𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} achieves robust and continual adaptation to emerging attacks under a noisy few-shot regime.

IV-A NIDS Workflow

The NIDS Workflow in Fig. 1 outlines the end-to-end process through which raw network traffic is transformed into discriminative feature representations for attack detection. It consists of three sequential modules—Flow Processor, Feature Encoder, and Attack-Traffic Classifier—described below.

Flow Processor. This module transforms raw network traffic into structured traffic data, which then serves as input to the Feature Encoder. The transformation occurs through two main steps: (i) Biflow Splittingand (ii) Input Extraction. In the first step, raw network traffic is organized into bidirectional flows (i.e. biflows). A biflow is formed by merging two unidirectional flows that share the same five-tuple (i.e. source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port, protocol) but travel in opposite directions. This aggregation provides a unified representation of bidirectional communication and avoids redundant flow entries [49, 7, 9, 11]. In the second step, only the first MpM_{p} packets of each biflow are retained. This approach enables early detection (Sec. II). By doing so, the NIDS can operate without waiting for the entire biflow to end, making it well-suited for real-time detection [7, 9, 11, 49]. From the MpM_{p} packets, MfM_{f} per-packet features (e.g., packet length and direction) are extracted to form the structured representation. Each biflow is thus represented as an Mp×MfM_{p}\times M_{f} feature matrix 𝒙\bm{x}. If fewer than MpM_{p} packets are available, zero-padding is applied to ensure 𝒙∈ℝMp×Mf\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{M_{p}\times M_{f}}, and the resulting matrix is normalized to [0,1][0,1] using Min–Max scaling.

Feature Encoder. The Feature Encoder maps each biflow matrix 𝒙∈ℝMp×Mf\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{M_{p}\times M_{f}} into a FF-dimensional feature embedding 𝐞=fθ​(𝒙)∈ℝF\mathbf{e}=f_{\theta}(\bm{x})\in\mathbb{R}^{F}, where fθf_{\theta} denotes the encoder parameterized by θ\theta. It serves as the backbone representation extractor of 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN}. Structurally, the encoder follows a symmetric U-Net–based architecture enhanced with residual connections [34]. The feature encoder consists of LL downsampling stages and the corresponding LL upsampling stages. Each downsampling stage LiL_{i} is constructed using a Residual Convolution Block (RCB) comprising two 2D convolutional layers, batch normalization, and LeakyReLU activations, with an identity skip path to stabilize gradient propagation. In the downsampling path, the input 𝒙\bm{x} is first reshaped to [1,Mp,Mf][1,M_{p},M_{f}] to match the 2D convolutional format, and processed by an initial RCB to yield a feature map of size [C​h0,Mp,Mf][Ch_{0},M_{p},M_{f}]. The feature map is passed through LL downsampling stages. Each stage progressively reduces the spatial resolution by pooling while doubling the number of feature channels. The output of the ii-th downsampling stage (i∈[1,L]i\in[1,L]) has the shape [Chi,MP//2i,Mf//2i][Ch_{i},M_{P}//2^{i},M_{f}//2^{i}], where /⁣/// denotes floor division, i.e. , MP//2i=⌊MP/2i⌋M_{P}//2^{i}=\left\lfloor M_{P}/2^{i}\right\rfloor. The resulting tensor is flattened and linearly projected to a fixed-length latent vector 𝐞∈ℝF\mathbf{e}\in\mathbb{R}^{F}, which compactly encodes both local packet-level and global flow-level patterns. In the upsampling path, each stage performs transposed convolution to restore the spatial resolution. Upsampled feature maps are concatenated with the corresponding outputs from the downsampling stages through skip connections, restoring finer details. Symmetrically, the output of the ii-th upsampling stage has the shape [ChL−i,MP//2L−i,Mf//2L−i][Ch_{L-i},M_{P}//2^{L-i},M_{f}//2^{L-i}]. Finally, a 1×11\times 1 convolution layer produces the reconstructed feature map of size [1,Mp,Mf][1,M_{p},M_{f}], which is used as auxiliary outputs for the reconstruction-based strategy in the base training phase.

Attack-Traffic Classification. The Attack-Traffic Classifier is a decision-making component that operates on the feature embeddings generated by the encoder (𝐞∈ℝF\mathbf{e}\in\mathbb{R}^{F}). Its objective is to classify benign traffic and multiple attack classes (viz. multi-class misuse detection [22]). Formally, in a generic incremental phase tt, we train the classifier using the embedded biflows from both the previously learned classes 𝒞old(t)\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{old}} and new ones 𝒞new(t)\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{new}}, where each class provides only KK labeled biflows. The classifier takes the embedding vector 𝐞\mathbf{e} as input and outputs a probability vector 𝐲^\hat{\mathbf{y}} over all observed classes 𝒞all(t)=𝒞old(t)∪𝒞new(t)\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{all}}=\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{old}}\cup\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{new}}. This mapping can be formally expressed as fcls:ℝF→ℝ|𝒞all(t)|f_{\mathrm{cls}}:\mathbb{R}^{F}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{all}}|}, where |𝒞all(t)||\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{all}}| denotes the total number of classes. For 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN}, we consider two possible lightweight classifiers, each offering complementary advantages in terms of stability and adaptability. (i) The Nearest-Neighbor (𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN}) classifier assigns each embedding to the class of its closest sample in the learned feature space. Here, we use a soft 𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN} rule, computing class posterior probabilities via a distance-based softmax over the nearest biflow from each class. This non-parametric approach relies on similarity measures and requires no trainable parameters, ensuring stability and low computational cost. (ii) The Logistic Regression (𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR}) classifier is a parametric linear model that learns decision boundaries by optimizing a cross-entropy objective. It provides greater discriminative power and flexibility, especially when sufficient labeled biflows are available. These two classifiers can be selected depending on the task configuration and the desired trade-off between stability and plasticity.

IV-B Learning Procedure

Fig. 1 illustrates the learning procedure of 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN}, describing how the NIDS learns and adapts across sequential phases. In particular, we consider two phases, i.e. Base Training Phase and Incremental Learning Phase, outlined hereinafter.

Base Training Phase. The goal of the base training phase is to construct an effective feature encoder on the base dataset, which consists of known attack classes and benign traffic classes (denoted as 𝒞base\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{base}}) with ample samples, to learn robust and transferable feature representations from network traffic. Once trained, this feature encoder serves as a teacher model that provides guidance for subsequent incremental phases. To ensure that the encoder learns discriminative and generalizable feature embeddings on 𝒞base\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{base}}, we jointly utilize supervised and self-supervised learning objectives and design three pretraining strategies (see Fig. 2).

  • •

    Reconstruction-based Strategy. According to this strategy, the feature extractor is mirrored to form a decoder gϕ​(⋅)g_{\phi}(\cdot) that reconstructs the input tensor 𝒙\bm{x} from the embedding vector 𝐞=fθ​(𝒙)\mathbf{e}=f_{\theta}(\bm{x}). It corresponds to the upsampling path of the U-Net architecture (see Sec. IV-A), where transposed convolutions and skip connections are employed to reconstruct the spatial-temporal structure of a biflow. In addition, a temporary classification head hψ​(⋅)h_{\psi}(\cdot) outputs attack-traffic prediction using the embedding 𝐞\mathbf{e}. The model is optimized by jointly minimizing the reconstruction loss and the classification loss (i.e. cross-entropy loss) (see Fig. 2):

    ℒrecon\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}} =∥𝒙−𝒙^∥22,ℒCE=−∑yclog(hψ(𝐞))\displaystyle=\|\bm{x}-\hat{\bm{x}}\|_{2}^{2},\quad\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}=-\sum y_{c}\log(h_{\psi}(\mathbf{e})) (4)
    ℒTotal\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{Total}} =α⋅ℒrecon+(1−α)⋅ℒCE\displaystyle=\alpha\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}}+(1-\alpha)\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}

    where 𝒙^=gϕ​(fθ​(𝒙))\hat{\bm{x}}=g_{\phi}(f_{\theta}(\bm{x})) is the reconstructed input, ycy_{c} represents the true label for class cc, and α\alpha is a balancing coefficient.

  • •

    Contrastive Strategy. The following strategy introduces a contrastive learning objective to encourage invariant and generalizable representations. Specifically, we adopt the Momentum Contrast (MoCo) [16], where 𝐞q\mathbf{e}_{q} denotes the query embedding produced by the encoder, 𝐞p\mathbf{e}_{p} is the positive embedding obtained from the momentum encoder (an augmented view of the same biflow), and {𝐞n(i)}i=1Nneg\{\mathbf{e}_{n}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{neg}}} are negative embeddings stored in a dynamic memory queue. The contrastive loss is formulated as:

    ℒContrast=−log⁡exp⁡(𝐞q⋅𝐞p/τ)exp⁡(𝐞q⋅𝐞p/τ)+∑i=1Nnegexp⁡(𝐞q⋅𝐞n(i)/τ),\mathcal{L}_{\text{Contrast}}=-\log\frac{\exp(\mathbf{e}_{q}\cdot\mathbf{e}_{p}/\tau)}{\exp(\mathbf{e}_{q}\cdot\mathbf{e}_{p}/\tau)+\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{neg}}}\exp(\mathbf{e}_{q}\cdot\mathbf{e}_{n}^{(i)}/\tau)}, (5)

    where τ>0\tau>0 is a temperature parameter controlling the softness of the probability distribution and 𝐞q⋅𝐞p\mathbf{e}_{q}\cdot\mathbf{e}_{p} denotes the inner product between two embedding vectors. We generate positive samples via a biflow-specific augmentation, called permutation, in which the original biflow is divided into nn segments and randomly reordered, simulating variations in packet sequencing [40]. The overall loss combines the contrastive and classification losses:

    ℒTotal=β⋅ℒContrast+(1−β)⋅ℒCE,\mathcal{L}_{\text{Total}}=\beta\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\text{Contrast}}+(1-\beta)\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}, (6)

    where β\beta is a balancing coefficient. This strategy enhances the invariance and generalization capability of the learned embeddings by contrasting positive and negative pairs across dynamic batches.

  • •

    Hybrid Strategy. This strategy combines the reconstruction and contrastive losses with the classification loss to fully exploit complementary supervision from multiple objectives, thereby improving the discriminability and robustness of the feature encoder. The overall loss function is formulated as:

    ℒTotal=α⋅ℒRecon+β⋅ℒContrast+(1−α−β)⋅ℒCE.\mathcal{L}_{\text{Total}}=\alpha\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\text{Recon}}+\beta\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\text{Contrast}}+(1-\alpha-\beta)\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}. (7)

Incremental Learning Phase. At each incremental phase tt, we adopt the 𝚁𝙵𝚂\mathtt{RFS} approach [39], using the feature extractor from the previous (t−1)t​h(t\!-\!1)^{th} phase as a teacher model to distill knowledge into the new student feature extractor fθ(t)f_{\theta^{(t)}}. In this phase, training relies exclusively on the biflows of previously learned classes stored in the memory, with the goal of preserving the stability of their feature representations. Formally, given the teacher model fθ(t−1)f_{\theta^{(t-1)}} from the previous phase (t−1)(t\!-\!1), we update the student fθ(t)f_{\theta^{(t)}} using only the classes 𝒞old(t)\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{old}} from phase (t−1)(t\!-\!1). Let 𝒟old(t)\mathcal{D}_{\text{old}}^{(t)} denote the training set containing 𝒞old(t)\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{old}} biflows selected by 𝙼𝚎𝚖​+\mathtt{Mem}\text{+} from the memory bank, the student is optimized by a weighted sum of the classification and KL distillation objectives:

θ(t)=argminθ(t)𝔼(𝒙,y)∼𝒟old(t)[\displaystyle\theta^{(t)}=\arg\min_{\theta^{(t)}}\;\mathbb{E}_{(\bm{x},y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{old}}^{(t)}}\Big[ λ1⋅ℒCE​(hψ(t)​(fθ(t)​(𝒙)),y)\displaystyle\,\lambda_{1}\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}\!\big(h_{\psi^{(t)}}(f_{\theta^{(t)}}(\bm{x})),\,y\big)
+λ2⋅ℒKL(hψ(t)\displaystyle+\lambda_{2}\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\big(h_{\psi^{(t)}} (fθ(t)(𝒙)),hψ(t−1)(fθ(t−1)(𝒙)))].\displaystyle(f_{\theta^{(t)}}(\bm{x})),\,h_{\psi^{(t-1)}}(f_{\theta^{(t-1)}}(\bm{x}))\big)\Big]. (8)

After convergence, during the tt​ht^{th} phase, we freeze the feature extractor fθ(t)f_{\theta^{(t)}} of the student to avoid catastrophic forgetting. The frozen model is then used to extract biflow embeddings 𝐞\mathbf{e} for the attack-traffic classifier (see Sec. IV-A). Finally, the updated student parameters θ(t)\theta^{(t)} replace the previous teacher for the next incremental phase (t+1)(t\!+\!1).

Memory Update (Mem+). After each incremental phase, the exemplar memory is updated to retain the most representative biflows for all learned classes. We denote the proposed enhanced exemplar selection as 𝙼𝚎𝚖​+\mathtt{Mem}\text{+}. For each class, we compute feature embeddings using the current model and select the KK most representative samples. 𝙼𝚎𝚖​+\mathtt{Mem}\text{+} supports multiple strategies: Herding [31], Rainbow [3], and random sampling. The memory size is bounded by a fixed budget, ensuring balanced representation across old and new classes. The updated memory bank is then used for the incoming incremental phase to support student training.

IV-C Noise-Aware Module

The Noise-Aware Module is the core component of our 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} framework. It operates only during the incremental learning phase to handle potential spurious labels in newly introduced attack classes, improving robustness in the 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL}-NIDS setting. It consists of two key components: (i) a Noise Detection Module, which detects and removes mislabeled samples, and (ii) a Feature Sampling Module, which synthesizes additional clean feature embeddings to maintain the original data scale and class balance.

Noise Detection Module. During the tt​ht^{th} incremental learning phase, for each new attack class c∈𝒞new(t)c\in\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{new}} with feature embeddings 𝐄c={𝐞1,…,𝐞K}\mathbf{E}_{c}=\{\mathbf{e}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{e}_{K}\}, we obtain a denoised subset 𝐄^c⊂𝐄c\widehat{\mathbf{E}}_{c}\subset\mathbf{E}_{c} by filtering out suspected mislabeled items using a denoising strategy. We remove the top κ=⌊ρ​K⌋\kappa=\lfloor\rho K\rfloor anomaly samples, where ρ∈[0,1]\rho\in[0,1] is a hyperparameter that controls the denoising ratio (i.e. the proportion of samples regarded as noisy). To achieve this goal, we explore four noise detection approaches, each designed to identify noisy samples from different statistical or representation-based perspectives.

  1. i)

    Local Outlier Factor (𝙻𝙾𝙵\mathtt{LOF}) evaluates the local density deviation of a biflow relative to its neighbors:

    LOFr​(𝐞i)=1|Nr​(𝐞i)|​∑𝐞j∈Nr​(𝐞i)lrdr​(𝐞j)lrdr​(𝐞i).\mathrm{LOF}_{r}(\mathbf{e}_{i})=\frac{1}{|N_{r}(\mathbf{e}_{i})|}\sum_{\mathbf{e}_{j}\in N_{r}(\mathbf{e}_{i})}\frac{\mathrm{lrd}_{r}(\mathbf{e}_{j})}{\mathrm{lrd}_{r}(\mathbf{e}_{i})}. (9)

    Here, Nr​(𝐞i)N_{r}(\mathbf{e}_{i}) denotes the rr-nearest neighbors of 𝐞i\mathbf{e}_{i}, where rr controls the neighborhood size, and lrdr​(⋅)\mathrm{lrd}_{r}(\cdot) is the local reachability density.

  2. ii)

    Isolation Forest (𝙸𝙵\mathtt{IF}) measures the expected isolation path length of each biflow:

    s⁡(𝐞i)=2−E⁡[L⁡(𝐞i)]ζ⁡(K),s(\mathbf{e}_{i})=2^{-\frac{E[L(\mathbf{e}_{i})]}{\zeta(K)}}, (10)

    where E⁡[L⁡(𝐞i)]E[L(\mathbf{e}_{i})] is the expected path length of 𝐞i\mathbf{e}_{i} in the isolation trees, and ζ⁡(K)\zeta(K) is a normalization factor depending on the sample size KK.

  3. iii)

    Prototype-Margin (𝙿𝚛𝚘𝚝𝚘𝙼𝚊𝚛𝚐𝚒𝚗\mathtt{ProtoMargin}) iteratively refines the class prototype and measures each biflow’s similarity margin between intra- and inter-class prototypes. The prototype is updated as:

    pc(0)\displaystyle p_{c}^{(0)} =1K​∑i=1K𝐞i,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\mathbf{e}_{i}, (11)
    pc(t+1)\displaystyle p_{c}^{(t+1)} =mean⁡(Top​-​r⁡{𝐞i∣sim⁡(𝐞i,pc(t))}),\displaystyle=\mean\big(\Topr\{\mathbf{e}_{i}\mid\simop(\mathbf{e}_{i},p_{c}^{(t)})\}\big), (12)

    where r=(1−ρ)​Kr=(1-\rho)K, and sim⁡(⋅,⋅)\simop(\cdot,\cdot) denotes the similarity function (e.g., cosine similarity). After II iterations, the score of each biflow is computed as:

    s⁡(𝐞i)=sim⁡(𝐞i,pc)−maxc′≠c⁡sim⁡(𝐞i,pc′).s(\mathbf{e}_{i})=\simop(\mathbf{e}_{i},p_{c})-\max_{c^{\prime}\neq c}\simop(\mathbf{e}_{i},p_{c^{\prime}}). (13)

    The top (1−ρ)​K(1-\rho)K biflows with the highest scores are retained as clean samples.

  4. iv)

    Example-Level Curriculum Learning (𝙴​-​𝙲𝙻\mathtt{E\text{-}CL}) trains a temporary classifier fϕf_{\phi} for a few epochs across all observed classes 𝒞all(t)\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{all}} [28]. The cross-entropy loss for a biflow 𝐞i\mathbf{e}_{i} with label y~i\tilde{y}_{i} is:

    ℓi=−log⁡exp⁡(fϕ​(𝐞i)​[y~i])∑j=1|𝒞all(t)|exp⁡(fϕ​(𝐞i)​[j]).\ell_{i}=-\log\frac{\exp(f_{\phi}(\mathbf{e}_{i})[\tilde{y}_{i}])}{\sum_{j=1}^{|\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{all}}|}\exp(f_{\phi}(\mathbf{e}_{i})[j])}. (14)

    Here, exp⁡(fϕ​(𝐞i)​[y~i])\exp(f_{\phi}(\mathbf{e}_{i})[\tilde{y}_{i}]) represents the probability score of sample 𝐞i\mathbf{e}_{i} on its observed label y~i\tilde{y}_{i} in the classifier output. The biflows with the highest ℓi\ell_{i} values are regarded as noisy and removed from the training set.

Feature Sampling Module. Since denoising reduces the number of training biflows, the Feature Sampling Module compensates for this loss by synthesizing new and clean feature embeddings. For each new attack class cc, it estimates and calibrates a Gaussian distribution from the denoised subset 𝐄^c\widehat{\mathbf{E}}_{c}:

μc=1|𝐄^c|​∑𝐞∈𝐄^c𝐞,Σc=Cov⁡(𝐄^c).\mu_{c}=\frac{1}{|\widehat{\mathbf{E}}_{c}|}\sum_{\mathbf{e}\in\widehat{\mathbf{E}}_{c}}\mathbf{e},\quad\Sigma_{c}=\Cov(\widehat{\mathbf{E}}_{c}). (15)

To enhance distributional stability, we adapt the estimated Gaussian parameters by fusing the distributional statistics of base classes 𝒞base\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{base}} into the attack class cc. Let (μb,Σb)(\mu_{b},\Sigma_{b}) denote the mean and covariance of a base class b∈𝒞baseb\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{base}}, and let NbN_{b} be the number of samples. The similarity between class bb and cc is measured by the Euclidean distance db=‖μc−μb‖2d_{b}=\|\mu_{c}-\mu_{b}\|_{2}. We assign normalized weights to these base classes as:

ωb=1/(Nb⋅db)∑b∈𝒞base1/(Nb⋅db).\omega_{b}=\frac{1/(N_{b}\cdot d_{b})}{\sum_{b\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{base}}}1/(N_{b}\cdot d_{b})}. (16)

The calibrated Gaussian parameters are then computed as:

μc′\displaystyle\mu_{c}^{\prime} =ε​∑b∈𝒞baseωb​μb+(1−γ)​μc,\displaystyle=\varepsilon\sum_{b\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{base}}}\omega_{b}\,\mu_{b}+(1-\gamma)\mu_{c}, (17)
Σc′\displaystyle\Sigma_{c}^{\prime} =ε​∑b∈𝒞baseωb​Σb+(1−γ)​Σc+𝐈,\displaystyle=\varepsilon\sum_{b\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{base}}}\omega_{b}\,\Sigma_{b}+(1-\gamma)\Sigma_{c}+\mathbf{I}, (18)

where ε∈[0,1]\varepsilon\in[0,1] and γ∈[0,1]\gamma\in[0,1] control the fusion ratio. Finally, κ=⌊ρ​K⌋\kappa=\lfloor\rho K\rfloor synthetic embeddings are sampled from 𝒩⁡(μc′,Σc′)\mathcal{N}(\mu_{c}^{\prime},\Sigma_{c}^{\prime}) and added to the denoised subset 𝐄^c\widehat{\mathbf{E}}_{c} to restore a total of KK samples per class. This calibrated Gaussian sampling strategy effectively preserves discriminative and stable feature representations under both label noise and few-shot conditions.

V Experimental Setup

In this section, we present the experimental setup adopted in our evaluation. Sec. V-A describes the threat model and the related dataset. Next, Sec. V-B reports the main characteristics defining the 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL} setup. Finally, Sec. V-C introduces the performance metrics.

V-A Threat Model & Datasets

In this paper, we tackle a threat model based on flooding, information gathering, brute-force, injection, man-in-the-middle, and malware attacks.

  • •

    Flooding attacks aim to make targeted resources unavailable by overwhelming them with a large volume of traffic. Flooding is particularly dangerous in IoT environments, where compromised devices can be organized into botnets that generate massive coordinated traffic.

  • •

    Information Gathering includes activities aimed at discovering vulnerabilities, weak points, and sensitive information about a target resource that can be later exploited.

  • •

    Brute-Force attacks refer to an effort to gain unauthorized access to a system by systematically attempting multiple username and password combinations.

  • •

    Injection involves uploading malicious input to a system in order to manipulate its execution logic, access sensitive information, or execute unauthorized commands.

  • •

    Man-In-The-Middle (MITM) attacks occur when an adversary secretly intercepts the communication between two parties, allowing the attacker to eavesdrop on sensitive data or manipulate transmitted information.

  • •

    Malware refers to malicious code that, once installed on a victim system, can perform harmful actions such as stealing sensitive information, disrupting system operations, or enabling remote control by an attacker.

To represent this threat model, we selected three network intrusion detection datasets: 𝙲𝚂𝙴​-​𝙲𝙸𝙲​-​𝙸𝙳𝚂𝟸𝟶𝟷𝟾\mathtt{CSE\text{-}CIC\text{-}IDS2018} [35], 𝙴𝚍𝚐𝚎​-​𝙸𝙸𝚘𝚃\mathtt{Edge\text{-}IIoT} [12], and 𝙸𝚘𝚃​-​𝙽𝙸𝙳\mathtt{IoT\text{-}NID} [21]. This selection is motivated by the fact that they include attack classes aligned with the threat categories described above. Moreover, (i) they cover a wide range of attack scenarios across enterprise, IoT, and Industrial IoT (IIoT) environments; (ii) they are well-established and widely used in current literature [1, 9, 45, 10]; (iii) they are publicly available, ensuring reproducibility; and (iv) they are relatively recent, with the oldest dataset (𝙲𝚂𝙴​-​𝙲𝙸𝙲​-​𝙸𝙳𝚂𝟸𝟶𝟷𝟾\mathtt{CSE\text{-}CIC\text{-}IDS2018}) captured in 20182018 and the newest (𝙴𝚍𝚐𝚎​-​𝙸𝙸𝚘𝚃\mathtt{Edge\text{-}IIoT}) in 20222022.

The CSE-CIC-IDS2018 dataset is a widely used benchmark for intrusion detection [11, 45, 27, 9], released by the Canadian Institute for Cybersecurity. It contains realistic benign and attack traffic captured from a simulated enterprise network. The dataset includes 1313 classes (11 benign and 1212 attacks), covering attacks such as DoS, DDoS, Brute Force, Web attacks, and infiltration. Rather than relying on the released pre-computed features, we extract biflows directly from the PCAP traces and subsequently revise and clean the resulting dataset following the procedure described in [10]. The resulting dataset contains ≈109​k\approx 109k labeled biflows.

The Edge-IIoT dataset is designed for intrusion detection in industrial IoT environments. It captures traffic from edge computing scenarios with various industrial protocols (e.g., Modbus, MQTT). The dataset includes 1616 classes (11 benign and 1515 attack classes), covering botnets, ransomware, scanning, and various flooding attacks. Starting from the PCAPs, we perform a cleaning phase on 𝙴𝚍𝚐𝚎​-​𝙸𝙸𝚘𝚃\mathtt{Edge\text{-}IIoT} as in [6]. The final dataset consists of ≈731​k\approx 731k labeled biflows.

The IoT-NID dataset is collected from a realistic smart home environment, containing benign traffic and attacks on IoT devices such as SKT NUGU and EZVIZ Wi-Fi Camera. It includes 10 classes (11 benign and 99 attack classes), with attacks such as Mirai botnet, DoS, MITM, and port scanning. After the PCAP cleaning phase [6], it contains ≈197​k\approx 197k labeled biflows.

Fig. 3 shows the number of biflows per class for each dataset, colored according to the attack categories defined in the threat model and ranked in decreasing order.

V-B FSCIL Setup

This section describes the experimental setup used to evaluate our proposed approach. We detail the class-splitting criteria, evaluation protocol, hyperparameter settings, and implementation specifics to ensure reproducibility.

Class Splitting. All classes in each dataset are divided into base (𝒞base\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{base}}) and new classes (𝒞new(t)\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{new}}) according to the number of per-class biflows. Base classes, including benign traffic and the most frequent attacks, are used for base training, while the three classes with the fewest biflows (i.e. the rarest attacks) are treated as 𝒞new(t)\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{new}} during incremental learning. For simplicity, we consider a single incremental phase in the main experiments, while Appendix A-C extends the analysis to multiple incremental phases. Fig. 3 illustrates the class split via the hatched bars.

Evaluation Scenario. Following common practice in the literature [11, 10, 9, 5], we evaluate 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} in the 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL} setting over 100100 classification tests. Each test simulates a few-shot classification task involving base and new classes. For each task, we construct a training set containing few labeled per-class biflows (i.e. from 55 to 1010) and a test set with 4040 biflows per class. The training biflows of the base classes are retrieved from the memory buffer maintained by 𝙼𝚎𝚖​+\mathtt{Mem}\text{+}, while the training biflows of the novel classes are drawn from the corresponding dataset. This setup evaluates 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN}’s ability to adapt to new attack classes while preserving previously learned knowledge in the 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL} setting.

Hyperparameter Setup. For the Flow Processor (see Sec. IV-A), in line with previous literature [9, 8], we use the first 2020 packets of each biflow (MP=20M_{P}=20) and extract 66 features from each packet (MF=6M_{F}=6). These features include: (i) packet length, (ii) packet direction, (iii) TCP window size, (iv) inter-arrival time, (v) time-to-live (TTL), and (vi) TCP flags. For the feature encoder, we set the feature embedding size FF to 320320. The number of downsampling operation is configured as L=2L=2, with the corresponding channel sizes specified as C​h0=16Ch_{0}=16, C​h1=32Ch_{1}=32, and C​h2=64Ch_{2}=64. For training, we use a batch size of 6464 and the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 1×10−41\times 10^{-4}. Each model is trained for up to 100100 epochs with an early-stopping strategy (patience of 2020 epochs) to prevent overfitting. Hyperparameters are selected based on preliminary tuning analyses (omitted for brevity). All random seeds are fixed to 00 for reproducibility, and unless otherwise noted, the same hyperparameter configuration is applied across all datasets and models.11 1 Implementation Details. All experiments are conducted on a workstation running Debian Linux, equipped with an Intel® 13th Gen Core i7-13700KF CPU (2424 threads, 1616 cores, base frequency 800800 MHz, turbo frequency up to 5.45.4 GHz) and an NVIDIA® GeForce RTX 40904090 D GPU, with sufficient main memory under a single NUMA node. The software environment is based on Python 3.10 with the following key libraries: PyTorch 1.12.1, PyTorch Lightning 1.0.2, Learn2Learn 0.1.7, scikit-learn 1.3.2, and Matplotlib/Seaborn for visualization. All packages are installed from PyPI unless otherwise specified, and all experiments are executed within a controlled conda environment to ensure reproducibility. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Luffy-2000/NAFN.

V-C Performance Metrics

In this paper, we use two performance metrics: the macro F1-score (F1 in short) and pAUC (Partial Area Under the Curve). The definitions are as follows.

Macro F1-score. It evaluates the attack classification capabilities (i.e. multi-class classification of benign and attack-specific traffic) of the NIDS. It is the harmonic mean of per-class 𝙿𝚛𝚎𝚌𝚒𝚜𝚒𝚘𝚗\mathtt{Precision} and 𝚁𝚎𝚌𝚊𝚕𝚕\mathtt{Recall} (or True Positive Rate, 𝚃𝙿𝚁\mathtt{TPR}), averaged equally across both benign and malicious classes. This ensures a fair evaluation that is not skewed by class imbalance. It is defined as:

𝙵𝟷​-​𝚜𝚌𝚘𝚛𝚎=1|𝒞|​∑i=1|𝒞|2×𝙿𝚛𝚎𝚌𝚒𝚜𝚒𝚘𝚗i×𝚁𝚎𝚌𝚊𝚕𝚕i𝙿𝚛𝚎𝚌𝚒𝚜𝚒𝚘𝚗i+𝚁𝚎𝚌𝚊𝚕𝚕i,\mathtt{F1}\text{-}\mathtt{score}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}|}\sum_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{C}|}\frac{2\times\mathtt{Precision}_{i}\times\mathtt{Recall}_{i}}{\mathtt{Precision}_{i}+\mathtt{Recall}_{i}}, (19)

where 𝒞\mathcal{C} denotes the set of all classes.

pAUC. The Area Under the Curve (AUC) evaluates the detection capabilities of the NIDS, i.e. its ability to discriminate between benign and malicious traffic in a binary classification task, by summarizing performance across all possible decision thresholds. The Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve plots the 𝚃𝙿𝚁\mathtt{TPR} against the False Positive Rate (𝙵𝙿𝚁\mathtt{FPR}, which represents false alarms), and the AUC is the area under this curve. While the AUC provides a comprehensive view of classifier performance, it includes high-𝙵𝙿𝚁\mathtt{FPR} regions, which are undesirable in practical NIDS deployments where excessive false positives may lead to blocking benign traffic. To better reflect realistic operational constraints, we therefore adopt the standardized pAUC, which restricts the AUC to a low-𝙵𝙿𝚁\mathtt{FPR} range. Specifically, we consider a maximum 𝙵𝙿𝚁\mathtt{FPR} of r=0.01​(1%)r=0.01~(1\%), viz.:

𝚙𝙰𝚄𝙲=12​(1+∫0r𝚃𝙿𝚁⁡(𝙵𝙿𝚁)​𝑑𝙵𝙿𝚁−r2/2r−r2/2),\mathtt{pAUC}=\frac{1}{2}\left(1+\frac{\int_{0}^{r}\mathtt{TPR}(\mathtt{FPR})\,d\mathtt{FPR}-r^{2}/2}{r-r^{2}/2}\right), (20)

which standardizes the partial area such that 𝚙𝙰𝚄𝙲=0.5\mathtt{pAUC}=0.5 indicates random performance and 𝚙𝙰𝚄𝙲=1.0\mathtt{pAUC}=1.0 indicates perfect classification. In the following, F1 and pAUC are averaged over 100100 classification tasks and reported with standard deviations to assess stability.

VI Experimental Results

In this section, we present the empirical evaluation of 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN}. Specifically, Sec. VI-A investigates different pretraining and memory selection strategies. Sec. VI-B analyzes the sensitivity of the NIDS to the number of shots (i.e. labeled biflows from novel attacks). Sec. VI-C examines training and inference efficiency. Secs. VI-D, VI-E and VI-F study robustness and feature separability under label noise. Finally, Sec. VI-G evaluates the cross-network incremental detection performance of 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} under label noise.

VI-A Evaluation Results under Different Pretraining Strategies and Memory Selection Methods

This experiment addresses  (Sec. III), namely whether 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} can adapt to new attack classes while retaining previously learned knowledge. To this end, we evaluate different combinations of pretraining and memory selection strategies (𝙼𝚎𝚖​+\mathtt{Mem}\text{+}) across three datasets to determine the optimal configuration under few-shot conditions. In the incremental learning phase, new attack classes from the same dataset as the base classes are introduced, each containing K=10K=10 labeled biflows. Table II reports F1-scores for new (F1-New), old (F1-Old), and all classes (F1-All).

Overall, the 𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN} classifier outperforms the 𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR} by an average of 1.37% F1-All. Therefore, the following analyses focus on the results obtained with the 𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN} classifier, while observations regarding 𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR} will only be briefly mentioned.

Performance on CSE-CIC-IDS2018. Hybrid + Random achieves the best overall performance, with F1-New=93.44%93.44\%, F1-Old=98.40%98.40\%, and F1-All=97.16%97.16\% (see Table II(a)). 𝙲𝚂𝙴​-​𝙲𝙸𝙲​-​𝙸𝙳𝚂𝟸𝟶𝟷𝟾\mathtt{CSE\text{-}CIC\text{-}IDS2018} contains complex and fine-grained traffic patterns, where Hybrid pretraining provides richer representations by combining reconstruction and contrastive objectives, while Random memory selection avoids the bias of ranking-based heuristics and keeps the retained biflows sufficiently diversified for adaptation.

Performance on Edge-IIoT. The best performance is obtained through W/o pretraining + Herding configuration, achieving F1-New=82.19%82.19\%, F1-Old=80.82%80.82\%, and F1-All=81.09%81.09\% (see Table II(b)). The dataset contains diverse and noisy traffic behaviors, so selecting representative biflows via Herding preserves overall stability. Other pretraining strategies show limited gains or even degradation in F1-New.

Performance on IoT-NID. Contrastive + Rainbow achieves the best overall performance, with F1-New=86.05%86.05\%, F1-Old=97.11%97.11\%, and F1-All=93.79%93.79\% (see Table II(c)). Contrastive pretraining yields discriminative features, while Rainbow memory selection enhances exemplar diversity, jointly supporting both new-class adaptation and old-class retention.

Takeaway. The optimal configuration varies across datasets due to differences in traffic characteristics. On 𝙲𝚂𝙴​-​𝙲𝙸𝙲​-​𝙸𝙳𝚂𝟸𝟶𝟷𝟾\mathtt{CSE\text{-}CIC\text{-}IDS2018}, Hybrid + Random (𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN}) and Contrastive + Rainbow (𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR}) perform best, benefiting from richer representations and informative memory selection. On 𝙴𝚍𝚐𝚎​-​𝙸𝙸𝚘𝚃\mathtt{Edge\text{-}IIoT}, W/o pretraining + Herding dominates for both classifiers, confirming that exemplar diversity outweighs feature initialization on this dataset. On 𝙸𝚘𝚃​-​𝙽𝙸𝙳\mathtt{IoT\text{-}NID}, contrastive pretraining is the key driver, with Contrastive + Rainbow (𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN}) and Contrastive + Random (𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR}) yielding the best trade-off between new- and old-class performance. In the following experiments, we will adopt these optimal configurations.

VI-B Sensitivity Analysis to the Number of Shots

The current section further explores by investigating how the number of shots (i.e. the number of labeled biflows per new attack class) affects the adaptation ability of 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN}. We assess the stability and scalability of the model as KK increases from 55 to 1010 shots, providing insight into the trade-off between sample availability and attack classification performance. As in the previous section, new and base classes belong to the same dataset, and we adopt the configuration selected in Sec. VI-A for each dataset. Fig. 4(a) and (b) show the F1-All achieved by 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} using the 𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN} and 𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR} classifiers, respectively, on the three datasets for varying numbers of shots.

For the 𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN} classifier (Fig. 4(a)), performance remains stable across different KK, with a slight improvement as KK increases. On 𝙲𝚂𝙴​-​𝙲𝙸𝙲​-​𝙸𝙳𝚂𝟸𝟶𝟷𝟾\mathtt{CSE\text{-}CIC\text{-}IDS2018}, F1-All stays above 92%92\%, rising marginally from 55 to 1010 shots. A similar trend appears on 𝙸𝚘𝚃​-​𝙽𝙸𝙳\mathtt{IoT\text{-}NID} (92%92\%–94%94\%), while 𝙴𝚍𝚐𝚎​-​𝙸𝙸𝚘𝚃\mathtt{Edge\text{-}IIoT} shows the lowest results (≈80%\approx 80\%), peaking at 81.2%81.2\% at K=9K=9.

For the 𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR} classifier (Fig. 4(b)), the benefit of larger KK is more evident. On 𝙲𝚂𝙴​-​𝙲𝙸𝙲​-​𝙸𝙳𝚂𝟸𝟶𝟷𝟾\mathtt{CSE\text{-}CIC\text{-}IDS2018}, performance improves from 87%87\%–88%88\% (55–77 shots) to nearly 94%94\% (99–1010 shots), a gain of ≈7%\approx 7\%. On 𝙸𝚘𝚃​-​𝙽𝙸𝙳\mathtt{IoT\text{-}NID}, the F1-All remains steady (92%92\%–93%93\%), while on 𝙴𝚍𝚐𝚎​-​𝙸𝙸𝚘𝚃\mathtt{Edge\text{-}IIoT}, the effect is stronger: F1-All increases from ≈71%\approx 71\% (55–77 shots) to 80%80\% (99–1010 shots), a gain exceeding 9%9\% F1-All.

Takeaway. As expected, the sensitivity analysis shows that increasing the number of shots improves performance for both classifiers, though the degree of improvement varies depending on the dataset. For 𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN}, the gains are relatively small yet consistent, whereas for 𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR}, the effect is more substantial, especially on 𝙲𝚂𝙴​-​𝙲𝙸𝙲​-​𝙸𝙳𝚂𝟸𝟶𝟷𝟾\mathtt{CSE\text{-}CIC\text{-}IDS2018} and 𝙴𝚍𝚐𝚎​-​𝙸𝙸𝚘𝚃\mathtt{Edge\text{-}IIoT}. These findings suggest that while more shots are beneficial overall, the sensitivity to sample size is highly dataset- and classifier-dependent.

VI-C Training and Inference Efficiency

To complement the analyses on , we measure the computational efficiency of 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} during both the base training and incremental phases. All timings are obtained with the per-dataset configuration selected in Sec. VI-A. Furthermore, we evaluate per-biflow inference latency to assess 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN}’s suitability for real-time NIDS deployment. We report the mean ±\pm standard deviation in seconds (for training) and microseconds (for inference) across the three considered datasets.

Table III shows that the incremental training phase consistently requires far less time than any of the pretraining procedures, regardless of the dataset or strategy. For instance, on 𝙲𝚂𝙴​-​𝙲𝙸𝙲​-​𝙸𝙳𝚂𝟸𝟶𝟷𝟾\mathtt{CSE\text{-}CIC\text{-}IDS2018}, the heaviest pretraining strategy (Hybrid) requires over 1,400.00​s1,400.00s, while student training completes in just 117.21​s117.21s. On 𝙴𝚍𝚐𝚎​-​𝙸𝙸𝚘𝚃\mathtt{Edge\text{-}IIoT}, which is the largest dataset, contrastive pretraining takes approximately 4,669.00​s4,669.00s, whereas incremental training finishes in only 666.75​s666.75s, which is less than 15%15\% of the cost. A similar pattern is observed on 𝙸𝚘𝚃​-​𝙽𝙸𝙳\mathtt{IoT\text{-}NID}, where even the lightest pretraining (W/o Pretraining, 456.39​s456.39s) still exceeds the adaptation time (346.19​s346.19s). Beyond the training efficiency, the bottom section of Table III highlights the real-time operational capacity of 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN}. Specifically, classifying a single incoming biflow requires merely 7.457.45–8.62​μ​s8.62\mu s using the 𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN} classifier, and 25.5425.54–33.25​μ​s33.25\mu s with the 𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR} classifier. This microsecond-level latency yields a theoretical throughput capable of processing tens to hundreds of thousands of biflows per second, ensuring that 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} will not become a bottleneck in high-speed networks.

Takeaway. These findings underscore the practicality of the teacher–student incremental framework, 𝚁𝙵𝚂\mathtt{RFS}. Once a teacher model has been pretrained, adapting a student model to new attack classes in the incremental training phase is both fast and computationally lightweight. Coupled with the low inference latency per biflow, this dual efficiency makes the 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} suitable for real-world NIDS deployments.

VI-D NAFN under Noisy Labels

This section addresses  by assessing the robustness of 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} to mislabeled biflows in the incremental data. Unless otherwise stated, each dataset uses the configuration selected in Sec. VI-A. We introduce controlled label noise in the new attack classes, with η=0%\eta=0\%–50%50\%, where η=0%\eta=0\% represents clean labels and higher values simulate increasingly severe label corruption. Unless otherwise specified, the denoising ratio is fixed at ρ=50%\rho=50\%. We compare four noise detection methods (Sec. IV-C)—𝙿𝚛𝚘𝚝𝚘𝙼𝚊𝚛𝚐𝚒𝚗\mathtt{ProtoMargin}, 𝙻𝙾𝙵\mathtt{LOF}, 𝙸𝙵\mathtt{IF}, and 𝙴​-​𝙲𝙻\mathtt{E\text{-}CL}—against a baseline without denoising approaches (briefly, 𝚠/𝚘​𝙳𝚎𝚗𝚘𝚒𝚜𝚎\mathtt{w/o~Denoise}). In addition, we include two noisy-label learning baselines: 𝙲𝚂𝙸𝙳𝙽\mathtt{CSIDN} [4] and 𝙽𝙲𝚁\mathtt{NCR} [18]. 𝙲𝚂𝙸𝙳𝙽\mathtt{CSIDN} assigns a reliability weight to each biflow based on predictive confidence, down-weighting samples with consistently low probabilities as potential noise. 𝙽𝙲𝚁\mathtt{NCR} addresses label noise through kk-NN topological consistency in the latent space, weighting samples according to agreement with their neighborhood and reducing the influence of isolated, inconsistent biflows. Herein, both new and base classes are drawn from the same dataset. Fig. 5 displays the performance in terms of F1-All, F1-New, and F1-Old.

Overall, performance declines as noise increases from η=10%\eta=10\% to 50%50\%, with the largest degradation on new attacks due to spurious labels. While 𝚠/𝚘​𝙳𝚎𝚗𝚘𝚒𝚜𝚎\mathtt{w/o~Denoise} shows high performance under low noise, its F1-New drops rapidly when noise exceeds 30%30\%, often dropping below 60%60\% and in some cases below 40%40\% at η=50%\eta=50\%. By contrast, 𝙿𝚛𝚘𝚝𝚘𝙼𝚊𝚛𝚐𝚒𝚗\mathtt{ProtoMargin} substantially improves robustness to noisy labels across all datasets and classifiers. For example, on 𝙲𝚂𝙴​-​𝙲𝙸𝙲​-​𝙸𝙳𝚂𝟸𝟶𝟷𝟾\mathtt{CSE\text{-}CIC\text{-}IDS2018} with 𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN}, 𝙿𝚛𝚘𝚝𝚘𝙼𝚊𝚛𝚐𝚒𝚗\mathtt{ProtoMargin} maintains an F1-New of 87.03%87.03\% at 50%50\% noise, compared with only 35.34%35.34\% of 𝚠/𝚘​𝙳𝚎𝚗𝚘𝚒𝚜𝚎\mathtt{w/o~Denoise}. Similarly, on 𝙴𝚍𝚐𝚎​-​𝙸𝙸𝚘𝚃\mathtt{Edge\text{-}IIoT}, 𝙿𝚛𝚘𝚝𝚘𝙼𝚊𝚛𝚐𝚒𝚗\mathtt{ProtoMargin} doubles the F1-New of the baseline under high noise conditions. Even with 𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR}, where improvements are generally smaller, 𝙿𝚛𝚘𝚝𝚘𝙼𝚊𝚛𝚐𝚒𝚗\mathtt{ProtoMargin} delivers consistent gains, highlighting that its effect is not limited to the 𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN} classifier. Importantly, 𝙿𝚛𝚘𝚝𝚘𝙼𝚊𝚛𝚐𝚒𝚗\mathtt{ProtoMargin} filters labels of noisy biflows from 𝒞new(t)\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{new}}, enhancing new-attack detection without significantly affecting knowledge of existing classes.

Compared with other noise detection methods, 𝙿𝚛𝚘𝚝𝚘𝙼𝚊𝚛𝚐𝚒𝚗\mathtt{ProtoMargin} exhibits superior stability and effectiveness. 𝙴​-​𝙲𝙻\mathtt{E\text{-}CL} shows some advantages with 𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR}, particularly under high noise, but it does not achieve the same gains on new attacks as 𝙿𝚛𝚘𝚝𝚘𝙼𝚊𝚛𝚐𝚒𝚗\mathtt{ProtoMargin}. 𝙻𝙾𝙵\mathtt{LOF} and 𝙸𝙵\mathtt{IF}, on the other hand, perform poorly, with F1-New scores often dropping below those of 𝚠/𝚘​𝙳𝚎𝚗𝚘𝚒𝚜𝚎\mathtt{w/o~Denoise}, indicating that generic outlier detection approaches are ill-suited for incremental scenarios where noise is structured and class-specific. It is worth noting that all methods yield lower F1-Old scores w.r.t. 𝚠/𝚘​𝙳𝚎𝚗𝚘𝚒𝚜𝚎\mathtt{w/o~Denoise}. Such a decline occurs because the denoising process inevitably introduces small perturbations to the decision boundaries of old classes, causing minor performance degradation. However, this drop is relatively modest and acceptable when weighed against the gains in F1-All scores. Furthermore, when evaluated against noisy-label learning baselines (𝙲𝚂𝙸𝙳𝙽\mathtt{CSIDN} and 𝙽𝙲𝚁\mathtt{NCR}), 𝙿𝚛𝚘𝚝𝚘𝙼𝚊𝚛𝚐𝚒𝚗\mathtt{ProtoMargin} continues to show clear advantages in the incremental setting. Although 𝙲𝚂𝙸𝙳𝙽\mathtt{CSIDN} and 𝙽𝙲𝚁\mathtt{NCR} exhibit some resilience against spurious labels w.r.t. 𝚠/𝚘​𝙳𝚎𝚗𝚘𝚒𝚜𝚎\mathtt{w/o~Denoise}, they struggle to adapt to new attacks under severe noise (e.g., η≥40%\eta\geq 40\%), resulting in sub-optimal F1-New. Moreover, lacking a denoising mechanism to preserve past knowledge, these baselines show a larger drop in F1-Old. Conversely, 𝙿𝚛𝚘𝚝𝚘𝙼𝚊𝚛𝚐𝚒𝚗\mathtt{ProtoMargin} better isolates noisy samples without distorting the decision boundaries, yielding superior F1-All. Overall, 𝙿𝚛𝚘𝚝𝚘𝙼𝚊𝚛𝚐𝚒𝚗\mathtt{ProtoMargin} achieves the best trade-off, it mitigates the effects of label noise on new attacks, sustains competitive overall F1-scores, and preserves stability on base classes.

At η=0%\eta=0\% and ρ=50%\rho=50\%, denoising causes a limited overall performance loss. Across all methods, the reduction in F1-All remains within ≈10%\approx 10\%, while F1-New and F1-Old decrease by up to approximately 32%32\% and 4%4\%, respectively, with occasional improvements in some settings. For 𝙿𝚛𝚘𝚝𝚘𝙼𝚊𝚛𝚐𝚒𝚗\mathtt{ProtoMargin}, F1-All typically decreases by only 1%1\%-5%5\% and F1-Old by less than 2%2\%, while F1-New shows a larger, dataset- and classifier-dependent drop of up to ≈20%\approx 20\%. Thus, even under the ρ=50%\rho=50\% setting, 𝙿𝚛𝚘𝚝𝚘𝙼𝚊𝚛𝚐𝚒𝚗\mathtt{ProtoMargin} incurs a limited cost on clean incremental data, mainly affecting new-class adaptation.

Takeaway. Addressing label noise in incremental learning is critical, as noise in new attacks can degrade overall performance. 𝙿𝚛𝚘𝚝𝚘𝙼𝚊𝚛𝚐𝚒𝚗\mathtt{ProtoMargin} is more stable than 𝚠/𝚘​𝙳𝚎𝚗𝚘𝚒𝚜𝚎\mathtt{w/o~Denoise}, other noise detection methods, and noisy-label baselines, especially at medium to high noise levels. Moreover, it preserves accuracy on new attacks while keeping base-class performance stable. Therefore, we adopt 𝙿𝚛𝚘𝚝𝚘𝙼𝚊𝚛𝚐𝚒𝚗\mathtt{ProtoMargin} as the core of the Noise-Aware Module.

VI-E Visual Analysis of NAFN

The following visualization experiment further supports  by illustrating how 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} enhances feature separability under noisy conditions. The analysis uses 𝙿𝚛𝚘𝚝𝚘𝙼𝚊𝚛𝚐𝚒𝚗\mathtt{ProtoMargin} as the noise detector, together with the per-dataset configuration selected in Sec. VI-A. Specifically, we visualize the confusion matrices and t-SNE projections of 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} using the 𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN} and 𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR} classifiers under η=50%\eta=50\% label noise, as well as the feature distributions of new attack classes.

Confusion Matrices. As shown in Fig. 6, each row corresponds to a dataset (𝙲𝚂𝙴​-​𝙲𝙸𝙲​-​𝙸𝙳𝚂𝟸𝟶𝟷𝟾\mathtt{CSE\text{-}CIC\text{-}IDS2018}, 𝙴𝚍𝚐𝚎​-​𝙸𝙸𝚘𝚃\mathtt{Edge\text{-}IIoT}, and 𝙸𝚘𝚃​-​𝙽𝙸𝙳\mathtt{IoT\text{-}NID}). The four columns report results for 𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN} (left) and 𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR} (right), both with and without 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} (with 𝙿𝚛𝚘𝚝𝚘𝙼𝚊𝚛𝚐𝚒𝚗\mathtt{ProtoMargin}). Across all datasets, label noise mainly affects new attacks located in the lower-right region of each confusion matrix. Without 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN}, classifiers exhibit greater confusion, as reflected by the fading of diagonal elements (which is particularly pronounced in 𝙴𝚍𝚐𝚎​-​𝙸𝙸𝚘𝚃\mathtt{Edge\text{-}IIoT} and 𝙸𝚘𝚃​-​𝙽𝙸𝙳\mathtt{IoT\text{-}NID}). On the other hand, with 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN}, misclassifications are greatly reduced, as can be seen from the diagonal. This outcome underscores that the Noise-Aware Module effectively filters mislabeled biflows and enhances intra-class consistency. Moreover, to address strict operational constraints, we report the binary detection performance (𝚃𝙿𝚁𝙵𝙿𝚁=1%\mathtt{TPR}_{\mathtt{FPR}=1\%}) above each subfigure. These metrics confirm that 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} not only recovers the fine-grained semantic boundaries of specific attacks, but also maintains a highly robust detection rate that approaches the theoretical upper bound achieved in the noiseless setting. Finally, the upper-left regions (𝒞base\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{base}}) remain stable under both noisy and denoised conditions, confirming that label noise primarily affects 𝒞new(t)\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{new}}.

t-SNE. Fig. 7 reports the Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) plots generated from 2D t-SNE projection, illustrating the feature distributions of new attack biflows under noisy conditions. Consistent with the setup in Fig. 6, each row corresponds to a dataset (𝙲𝚂𝙴​-​𝙲𝙸𝙲​-​𝙸𝙳𝚂𝟸𝟶𝟷𝟾\mathtt{CSE\text{-}CIC\text{-}IDS2018}, 𝙴𝚍𝚐𝚎​-​𝙸𝙸𝚘𝚃\mathtt{Edge\text{-}IIoT}, and 𝙸𝚘𝚃​-​𝙽𝙸𝙳\mathtt{IoT\text{-}NID}), while the four columns show the results of 𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN} and 𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR} classifiers, both with and without 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN}. Projections show that 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} substantially enhances feature separability across all three datasets. Specifically, when not using 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} (columns 11 and 33), the feature distributions of the three new classes almost completely overlap, making them indistinguishable. By contrast, with 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} (columns 22 and 44), the class-specific clusters are much more distinct, highlighting an improved discriminative structure of the feature space.

Takeaway. Confusion matrices and t-SNE provide a visual corroboration of the classification results: label noise mainly harms the detection of new attacks, while 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} effectively restores their separability, thereby improving robustness under noisy-label incremental-learning scenarios.

VI-F Analysis of Early Detection and Time-to-Insight of NAFN

To further address , we evaluate the real-time detection ability of 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} under label noise (η=50%\eta=50\%), confirming its effectiveness for early detection. This analysis focuses on 𝙲𝚂𝙴​-​𝙲𝙸𝙲​-​𝙸𝙳𝚂𝟸𝟶𝟷𝟾\mathtt{CSE\text{-}CIC\text{-}IDS2018} and uses the corresponding configuration selected in Sec. VI-A. In detail, we investigate the performance under varying time thresholds TsT_{s}, which directly dictate the Time-to-Insight (TTI). TTI is defined as the duration from the arrival of the initial packet of a biflow to its final classification [9], and it dominates inference latency, far exceeding the overhead of feature extraction and embedding. While lower TsT_{s} values enhance real-time responsiveness, they increase vulnerability to slow-rate flooding attacks; conversely, higher TsT_{s} values improve detection accuracy but delay biflow classification. In this analysis, we focus on 𝙲𝚂𝙴​-​𝙲𝙸𝙲​-​𝙸𝙳𝚂𝟸𝟶𝟷𝟾\mathtt{CSE\text{-}CIC\text{-}IDS2018} due to the presence of slow-rate flooding attacks.

Fig. 8 illustrates the confusion matrices and corresponding F1-All scores across Ts∈{1​s,5​s,10​s,50​s,100​s,𝙼𝙰𝚇b}T_{s}\in\{1s,5s,10s,50s,100s,\mathtt{MAX}_{b}\}, where 𝙼𝙰𝚇b=330​s\mathtt{MAX}_{b}=330s denotes the maximum flow duration. Despite noise interference, we observe a significant performance leap as TsT_{s} increases from 11s to 1010s (i.e. ≈+7%\approx+7\% F1-All for 𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN} and 𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR}). Beyond the 1010s mark, the detection performance enters a stable plateau, with gains below 1%1\%. Although the highest F1-All (95.00%95.00\% for 𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN} and 92.84%92.84\% for 𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR}) values are achieved at Ts=𝙼𝙰𝚇bT_{s}=\mathtt{MAX}_{b}, results show that Ts=50​sT_{s}=50s offers the best balance.

Takeaway. 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} reaches near-peak accuracy within 10​s\mathit{10s} and achieves the best trade-off at Ts=50​s\mathit{T_{s}=50s}, reducing detection latency by 6×\mathit{6\times} while remaining robust under 50%\mathit{50\%} label noise and effectively mitigating slow-rate attacks.

VI-G Cross-Network Incremental Detection Performance

This section tackles , focusing on whether 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} can consistently sustain robust and generalizable detection performance across diverse network environments. To this end, we evaluate the cross-network incremental detection capability of 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} by training on traffic from one dataset and incrementally introducing new attack classes from a different dataset, while using the same base and new classes defined in Sec. V-B. Base training uses, for each base dataset, the configuration selected in Sec. VI-A, and the incremental phase reuses the same encoder and classifier setup with the new classes drawn from the other dataset. To analyze performance under this cross-network setup, we report three distinct pAUCs. Each metric is defined based on the origin and role of the malicious classes involved. Specifically, (i) pAUCbase-mal\text{pAUC}_{\text{base-mal}}: evaluates the ability to retain discrimination between benign and base malicious traffic, where all attacks from the base dataset are grouped into a single malicious class (as explained in Sec. V-C); (ii) pAUCinc-mal\text{pAUC}_{\text{inc-mal}}: measures the ability to detect newly introduced malicious traffic from a different dataset during the incremental learning phase; (iii) pAUCunk-inc\text{pAUC}_{\text{unk-inc}}: assesses the detection of unseen malicious traffic from a different network environment. It considers the base classes of the incremental dataset which are observed neither during base training nor during the incremental phase, and are therefore unknown at test time. Table IV reports the three pAUCs for each base–incremental dataset pair, using the 𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN} and 𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR} classifiers. Results are shown without 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN}—both without noise (η=0%\eta=0\%) and with noise (η=50%\eta=50\%)—as well as for 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} with noise (η=50%\eta=50\%).

Regarding the 𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN} classifier (Table IV(a)), 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} exhibits strong detection performance according to all three pAUCs. Detection of base malicious classes remains consistently high, with pAUCbase-mal\text{pAUC}_{\text{base-mal}} values often exceeding 95%95\%, indicating that the NIDS effectively retains previous knowledge even in the presence of domain shifts. In contrast, the performance on pAUCinc-mal\text{pAUC}_{\text{inc-mal}} and pAUCunk-inc\text{pAUC}_{\text{unk-inc}} varies noticeably across dataset pairs. Particularly, combinations involving 𝙲𝚂𝙴​-​𝙲𝙸𝙲​-​𝙸𝙳𝚂𝟸𝟶𝟷𝟾\mathtt{CSE\text{-}CIC\text{-}IDS2018} and 𝙸𝚘𝚃​-​𝙽𝙸𝙳\mathtt{IoT\text{-}NID} show greater degradation, reflecting a larger distributional gap. Nonetheless, 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} mitigates the impact of label noise and domain shift, improving the detection of new and unknown attacks. For example, when adapting from 𝙸𝚘𝚃​-​𝙽𝙸𝙳\mathtt{IoT\text{-}NID} to 𝙲𝚂𝙴​-​𝙲𝙸𝙲​-​𝙸𝙳𝚂𝟸𝟶𝟷𝟾\mathtt{CSE\text{-}CIC\text{-}IDS2018}, 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} improves pAUCinc-mal\text{pAUC}_{\text{inc-mal}} from 84.00%84.00\% to 96.68%96.68\%, and pAUCunk-inc\text{pAUC}_{\text{unk-inc}} from 62.45%62.45\% to 73.13%73.13\%. Such gains highlight the effectiveness of 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} in noise filtering and stabilizing incremental adaptation.

The 𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR} classifier (Table IV(b)) exhibits a more stable yet slightly more conservative performance profile. Although pAUCbase-mal\text{pAUC}_{\text{base-mal}} is consistently high (above ≈95%\approx 95\%), the metrics involving cross-network generalization, namely pAUCinc-mal\text{pAUC}_{\text{inc-mal}} and pAUCunk-inc\text{pAUC}_{\text{unk-inc}}, show moderate drops, especially when 𝙸𝚘𝚃​-​𝙽𝙸𝙳\mathtt{IoT\text{-}NID} serves as either the base or incremental dataset. Despite this, 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} again provides consistent improvements in all settings, albeit with smaller margins w.r.t. 𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN}. These outcomes indicate that 𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR} benefits from noise-aware filtering, although its feature representation is inherently less sensitive to label noise than the 𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN} classifier.

Takeaway. Cross-network experiments show that both 𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN} and 𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR} can adapt to unseen attack classes from heterogeneous environments, with generalization varying by dataset pair. Across all three pAUCs, 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} consistently improves performance by mitigating label noise and enhancing robustness to unseen malicious biflows. These results indicate that 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} supports reliable incremental learning and strengthens cross-network transferability under both clean and noisy label conditions.

VII Conclusions & Future Perspectives

In this paper, we propose 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN}, a Noise-Aware Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning framework for Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDSs). 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} introduces a teacher–student adaptation approach and a Noise-Aware Module to enable continual adaptation to new attack classes while mitigating the detrimental effects of noisy labels.
