Through extensive evaluations across three benchmark datasets, we validate the effectiveness of 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} by addressing a comprehensive set of research questions (Sec. III). With regard to , our experiments show that 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} can efficiently adapt to new attacks under a few-shot regime while preserving performance on previously learned classes. For , the proposed Noise-Aware Module, via the Prototype-Margin method, significantly improves robustness against mislabeled biflows. At label-noise ratios ranging from 10%10\% to 50%50\%, the F1-score on new classes improves by up to +52%+52\% w.r.t. the baseline without denoising, consistently outperforming alternative noise detection methods while preserving the separability of new-class representations. Finally, regarding , our cross-network experiments reveal that 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} maintains stable and transferable detection capabilities across heterogeneous network environments. Even under severe label noise and pronounced domain shifts, 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} consistently improves cross-network incremental detection, with observed pAUC gains of up to 13%13\% and 11%11\% for new and previously unseen attacks, respectively.

Limitations & Future Avenues. The findings of this manuscript suggest several promising directions for future research to address the current limitations of 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN}. (i) Retransmissions and packet loss in dynamic network environments may alter traffic features, potentially affecting the robustness of 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN}. Future work could address this limitation through adaptive feature extraction or more robust representation learning techniques [20]. (ii) Traffic drift and memory bias accumulation during long-term incremental updates may be reduced by developing scalable memory management strategies or continual prototype calibration methods [51], improving model stability in online or extended deployments. (iii) Explainable AI can increase the transparency and interpretability of the model [6], enabling security operators to better understand detection decisions and enhancing usability in real-world scenarios. (iv) 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN}assumes that the presence of label noise is known; future work could detect label corruption through confidence monitoring or prototype consistency, automatically triggering the denoising pipeline. (v) The paper assumes a symmetric distribution of noise across the new classes. Future work could investigate asymmetric noise distributions based on attack-type similarity.

Appendix A Appendix

A-A Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis

In this section, we conduct a sensitivity analysis of the hyperparameters (ϵ,γ,ρ)(\epsilon,\gamma,\rho) related to the feature sampling module (Sec. IV-C). Specifically, ϵ\epsilon and γ\gamma control the fusion rates for the base classes CbaseC_{\text{base}} and the novel classes CnewC_{\text{new}} (cf. Eqs. 17 and 18), respectively, while ρ\rho controls the denoising ratio. We vary ϵ\epsilon and γ\gamma over the interval [0.1,0.9][0.1,0.9], while setting ρ\rho within [0.1,0.5][0.1,0.5]. Unless otherwise specified, the default setting is ϵ=γ=0.7\epsilon=\gamma=0.7 and ρ=0.5\rho=0.5. To isolate the effect of each factor, we adopt a one-at-a-time protocol: when tuning one hyperparameter, the others are fixed at their default values.

Fig. 9 shows the F1-All curves of 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} over the three hyperparameters on 𝙲𝚂𝙴​-​𝙲𝙸𝙲​-​𝙸𝙳𝚂𝟸𝟶𝟷𝟾\mathtt{CSE\text{-}CIC\text{-}IDS2018}, 𝙴𝚍𝚐𝚎​-​𝙸𝙸𝚘𝚃\mathtt{Edge\text{-}IIoT}, and 𝙸𝚘𝚃​-​𝙽𝙸𝙳\mathtt{IoT\text{-}NID}, using two classifiers (𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN} and 𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR}) under label noise with η=50%\eta=50\%. Overall, 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} remains stable across ϵ\epsilon and γ\gamma. Changing the fusion rates leads to only marginal performance fluctuations, suggesting that the model is weakly sensitive to the mixture weights between CbaseC_{\text{base}} and CnewC_{\text{new}}. In contrast, ρ\rho has a stronger effect since it controls the denoising strength. As ρ\rho increases, 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} achieves better detection performance under η=50%\eta=50\% label noise, implying that stronger denoising is beneficial when supervision is heavily corrupted. Notably, the best performance is obtained when ρ\rho is close to the true label-noise ratio η\eta, which aligns with the intuition that the denoising ratio should match the corruption level and further corroborates the effectiveness of the Noise-Aware Module. Meanwhile, 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} remains robust even with conservative denoising (e.g., ρ=0.1\rho=0.1). Despite 50%50\% noise, performance does not drop significantly, showing that the framework does not rely on aggressive denoising to work well.

In summary, 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} is largely insensitive to (ϵ,γ,ρ)(\epsilon,\gamma,\rho). In particular, ϵ\epsilon and γ\gamma can be chosen from a broad range without noticeable impact, while ρ\rho provides a controllable knob that adaptively improves performance as the noise level increases.

A-B Ablation of Feature Sampling Module

In the following, we ablate the post-denoising compensation stage. Specifically, after the noise detection module, we compare Denoise-only (no compensation) with three embedding-space compensation strategies: MixUp, SMOTE, and Ours (Gaussian embedding synthesis fitted on the remaining samples). Experiments are conducted on the three datasets, using 𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN} and 𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR}. Table V reports F1-All, F1-New, and F1-Old.

Overall, Denoise-only is insufficient and can significantly degrade performance after samples are filtered out. This issue is particularly pronounced for 𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR}, which relies on adequate coverage of the feature space. For instance, on 𝙲𝚂𝙴​-​𝙲𝙸𝙲​-​𝙸𝙳𝚂𝟸𝟶𝟷𝟾\mathtt{CSE\text{-}CIC\text{-}IDS2018} with 𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR}, Denoise-only yields only 78.66%78.66\% F1-All and 32.74%32.74\% F1-New, resulting in weaker generalization to new classes due to the lack of compensation. On the other hand, biflow compensation restores and often improves performance, suggesting that denoising and compensation play complementary roles: denoising improves sample reliability, while compensation mitigates the distribution gaps caused by filtering. Moreover, our Gaussian embedding synthesis (Denoise+Ours) performs on par with widely-used alternatives such as MixUp and SMOTE in embedding space. Notably, on 𝙲𝚂𝙴​-​𝙲𝙸𝙲​-​𝙸𝙳𝚂𝟸𝟶𝟷𝟾\mathtt{CSE\text{-}CIC\text{-}IDS2018} with 𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN}, Denoise+Ours achieves the best results (95.01%95.01\% F1-All and 87.02%87.02\% F1-New), slightly outperforming the baselines. These results confirm that post-denoising compensation is crucial for maintaining performance under few-shot filtering, and our approach provides competitive (and occasionally superior) gains relative to standard embedding-space augmentation methods.

A-C Multiple Incremental Results

To complement the single-session protocol used in the main evaluation, we further assess 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} under a multi-step incremental setting. For each dataset, the rare attack classes originally assigned to 𝒞new(t)\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{new}} are introduced sequentially over three incremental steps, with one new class added at each step. At step #​t\#t, the model is adapted using the available few-shot samples of the current new class, while the previously observed classes are retained through the memory buffer. The evaluation set then includes all classes observed up to that step, allowing us to measure both the adaptation to the newly introduced attack and the preservation of previously acquired knowledge. We keep the same experimental setup used in the main experiments; values are averaged over 100100 tasks and reported as mean F1-score with standard deviation.

Table VI shows that 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} remains effective beyond a single incremental session. Across datasets and classifiers, F1-Old stays stable after successive updates, indicating that 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} mitigates catastrophic forgetting even when new attacks are introduced one by one. This behavior is particularly clear on 𝙲𝚂𝙴​-​𝙲𝙸𝙲​-​𝙸𝙳𝚂𝟸𝟶𝟷𝟾\mathtt{CSE\text{-}CIC\text{-}IDS2018}, where 𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN} preserves F1-Old above 98%98\% across all three steps, and on 𝙸𝚘𝚃​-​𝙽𝙸𝙳\mathtt{IoT\text{-}NID}, where both classifiers retain more than 93%93\% F1-Old at the final step. The overall performance also remains competitive: after three incremental steps, 𝙽𝙰𝙵𝙽\mathtt{NAFN} achieves 97.18%97.18\%, 80.92%80.92\%, and 93.53%93.53\% F1-All with 𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN} on 𝙲𝚂𝙴​-​𝙲𝙸𝙲​-​𝙸𝙳𝚂𝟸𝟶𝟷𝟾\mathtt{CSE\text{-}CIC\text{-}IDS2018}, 𝙴𝚍𝚐𝚎​-​𝙸𝙸𝚘𝚃\mathtt{Edge\text{-}IIoT}, and 𝙸𝚘𝚃​-​𝙽𝙸𝙳\mathtt{IoT\text{-}NID}, respectively. The main limitation appears in F1-New when the final introduced class is substantially harder or less separable. For example, on 𝙴𝚍𝚐𝚎​-​𝙸𝙸𝚘𝚃\mathtt{Edge\text{-}IIoT}, F1-New reaches 100.00%100.00\% at step #​2\#2 but drops to 55.33%55.33\% for 𝙽𝙽\mathtt{NN} and 54.03%54.03\% for 𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR} at step #​3\#3. A similar, though milder, pattern appears on 𝙲𝚂𝙴​-​𝙲𝙸𝙲​-​𝙸𝙳𝚂𝟸𝟶𝟷𝟾\mathtt{CSE\text{-}CIC\text{-}IDS2018} with 𝙻𝚁\mathtt{LR}, where the final-step F1-New decreases to 76.20%76.20\%. These drops highlight that multi-step 𝙵𝚂𝙲𝙸𝙻\mathtt{FSCIL} performance depends not only on the number of sessions but also on the intrinsic separability and biflow quality of the newly introduced attack class. Nevertheless, the corresponding F1-Old remains high, showing that the performance loss is concentrated on the current new class rather than caused by broad forgetting.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
